title: Can GPT Be Used as an Alternative Prediction Model to Traditional Machine Learning and Neural Networks on Low-Volume Clinical Data?
authors: Bin Akter, S.; Akter, S.; Eisenberg, D.; Hill, C.; Lotvola, A.; Fresneda Fernandez, J.; Sarkar Pias, T.; Rafiqul Islam, M.; Islam, H.
abstract: Background and Objective: Early and reliable disease prediction from structured clinical data remains challenging when datasets are small, highly imbalanced, and contain limited positive disease cases. Conventional machine learning (ML) and deep learning approaches often struggle to capture clinically meaningful relationships under such low-data representation conditions due to weak statistical associations between features and prediction targets. This study proposes a clinically grounded GPT2-based table-to-text framework for disease prediction using structured healthcare datasets, motivated by the contextual reasoning capability of GPT models to better capture clinically meaningful relationships when statistical learning alone becomes insufficient due to limited data availability. Methods & Materials: Structured clinical records were transformed into physician-style textual descriptions and enriched through GPT4-generated medical paraphrasing to improve minority-class representation while preserving clinical meaning. Both the original and generated clinical texts were used to fine-tune a GPT2 model across four public healthcare datasets, including heart disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and thyroid cancer recurrence. Gradient-based explainable AI analysis was additionally incorporated to identify clinically important features influencing prediction outcomes. Results: The proposed framework demonstrated consistently strong predictive performance with average precision, specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.96, 0.97, 0.96, and 0.96, respectively. The model achieved improved sensitivity, stronger generalization, and more stable predictive behavior compared with traditional ML, deep learning, transformer-based, and GAN-augmented approaches. Importantly, the framework consistently emphasized clinically meaningful variables even under severe class imbalance where conventional ML and neural network models often struggled. Conclusions: The proposed GPT2-based table-to-text framework provides a practical and clinically interpretable approach for disease prediction from limited structured healthcare data. By integrating contextual clinical reasoning with explainable prediction mechanisms, the framework demonstrates strong potential for early risk detection, transparent clinical decision support, and reliable deployment in real-world low-resource healthcare environments.

infographic.key_insight: A GPT-2 table-to-text framework can outperform traditional ML and neural networks on small, imbalanced clinical datasets by turning structured records into clinically meaningful text for prediction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach may help improve early disease risk prediction from low-volume hospital data while keeping the output more interpretable for clinicians.
method: Converted structured clinical variables into physician-style text.
Used GPT-4 paraphrasing to augment minority-class examples while preserving medical meaning.
Fine-tuned GPT-2 on four public datasets and applied gradient-based explainability to identify important features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across heart disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and thyroid cancer recurrence datasets, the model reported average precision, specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.96, 0.97, 0.96, and 0.96.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from public benchmark datasets, so performance and clinical utility may differ in real-world settings with noisier data, different prevalence, or site-specific biases.
infographic.paper_title: Can GPT Be Used as an Alternative Prediction Model to Traditional Machine Learning and Neural Networks on Low-Volume Clinical Data?

title: COVID-19 vaccination and survival of cancer patients in Northwestern Russia: a historical registry-based cohort study
authors: Dyachenko, A. A.; Bogdanov, M. A.; Bogdanov, D. V.; Meldo, A. A.; Chernina, V. Y.; Gombolevskiy, V. A.; Grjibovski, A. M.; Valkov, M. Y.
abstract: BackgroundCancer patients face a significantly elevated risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes. Although vaccination is a cornerstone of prevention, data on vaccination coverage and association with survival among Russian cancer patients remain scarce. We assessed COVID-19 vaccination coverage and its association with overall survival in a population-based cohort of cancer patients in Northwest Russia. MethodsThis retrospective registry-based cohort study integrated data from the Population-Based Cancer Registry (PBCR) of the Arkhangelsk Region and the Nenets Autonomous Okrug, regional vaccination records, and an artificial intelligence (AI)-based analysis of chest computed tomography (CT) scans. The cohort consisted of 1,144 cancer patients who underwent CT between August 2020 and April 2021. Vaccination status was ascertained via data linkage. Overall survival (OS) was compared between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression, adjusted for demographic, clinical, and AI-derived CT biomarkers. To mitigate immortal time bias, the primary analysis used a landmark approach restricted to patients alive on March 1, 2021 (N = 1,136). A sensitivity analysis used a November 1, 2021 landmark (N = 894). Vaccination status was defined as receipt of at least one dose before the landmark date. ResultsOnly 6.6% (n=76) of patients received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine (Sputnik V or Sputnik Light). Vaccinated patients were more likely to have earlier-stage cancer and were less likely to be receiving active treatment. In the primary landmark analysis, vaccination was associated with a significantly higher 3-year OS (80.3% vs. 45.7%, p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, vaccination was independently associated with a 60% lower hazard of all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.25-0.64). AI-detected COVID-19 pneumonia on baseline CT was also an independent predictor of poorer survival (adjusted HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.09-1.59). In the sensitivity analysis (November 1, 2021 landmark), the adjusted HR for vaccination was 0.56 (95% CI 0.34-0.92), showing a consistent but attenuated association. ConclusionThis study reveals critically low COVID-19 vaccination coverage among cancer patients in Northwest Russia. Nevertheless, vaccination was strongly associated with a substantial survival benefit, underscoring its importance as a potentially lifesaving intervention for this vulnerable population.

infographic.key_insight: In this Northwestern Russia registry study, cancer patients who received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose had better overall survival than unvaccinated patients.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings suggest vaccination may be an important survival-associated preventive measure for cancer patients, especially those at higher risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes.
method: Retrospective population-based cohort linking cancer registry, vaccination records, and AI-analyzed chest CT data.
Primary landmark survival analysis among patients alive on March 1, 2021, with multivariable Cox adjustment.
Sensitivity analysis repeated with a later landmark date to reduce immortal time bias.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 1,144 cancer patients, only 6.6% were vaccinated, and vaccination was associated with improved 3-year overall survival and a lower adjusted mortality hazard.
infographic.watch_item: Because this is observational registry research, residual confounding and selection differences between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients may still influence the association.
infographic.paper_title: COVID-19 vaccination and survival of cancer patients in Northwestern Russia: a historical registry-based cohort study

title: Data-efficient machine learning for the detection of duodenal neoplasia: a multi-centre study
authors: Di Lisio, F.; Soilleux, E. J.; Jaeckle, F.
abstract: BackgroundMachine Learning (ML) has shown promise in histopathological diagnosis, but rare tumours, like duodenal epithelial neoplasms, are challenging because large, labelled datasets are difficult to assemble. We propose a data-efficient ML pipeline for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia in whole-slide images. MethodsWe assembled a five-hospital dataset of haematoxylin and eosin-stained duodenal biopsy whole slide images (WSIs) at 10x magnification, comprising 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic biopsies, including adenomas, carcinomas and neuroendocrine tumours. WSIs were divided into patches and encoded using the Hibou-B foundation model. We compared global standardisation with unsupervised site-specific standardisation of patch embeddings. Our pipeline combined principal component analysis, a Gaussian mixture model and a Random Forest classifier. We assessed generalisability using leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation across four hospitals and on an independent test set from a fifth hospital. ResultsIn leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation, the pipeline achieved a mean accuracy of 90%, sensitivity of 96%, specificity of 83% and an AUC of 0.96. On the external test hospital, it achieved 94% accuracy, 93% sensitivity, 95% specificity, and AUC of 0.97. Site-specific standardisation improved mean cross-validation accuracy by 20 percentage points compared with global standardisation, while the Gaussian mixture pipeline improved accuracy by 12 percentage points compared with mean pooling of patch embeddings. ConclusionsWe present a data-efficient ML approach for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia from WSIs. Strong performance was maintained across hospitals and on an independent external test cohort despite the limited number of neoplastic training cases, supporting the feasibility of foundation-model-based approaches for rare histopathological diagnoses.

infographic.key_insight: A foundation-model-based, data-efficient pipeline can detect rare duodenal epithelial neoplasia from whole-slide biopsy images with strong cross-site performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could help pathology labs screen rare duodenal lesions more reliably when labelled training data are limited.
method: Five-hospital H&E WSI dataset of 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic duodenal biopsies
Patch-level encoding with the Hibou-B foundation model plus PCA, Gaussian mixture modeling, and Random Forest classification
Compared global vs unsupervised site-specific standardisation and validated with leave-one-hospital-out and external testing
infographic.evidence_signal: The pipeline achieved 90% mean accuracy in leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation and 94% accuracy on an independent external hospital test set, with AUC up to 0.97.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was strong but the neoplastic class was still relatively small, so broader prospective validation is needed before routine deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Data-efficient machine learning for the detection of duodenal neoplasia: a multi-centre study

title: Developing an OMOP-Standardized Prostate Cancer Database and Improving Data Quality Using NLP and PSA-Based Algorithms
authors: Wang, J.; Jackson, J. C.; Garza, A.; Nalla, S.; Ninnemann, T.; Zhang, Y.; Kuo, Y.-F.
abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate an Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership-(OMOP-) standardized prostate cancer database from the University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) Epic Electronic Health Record (EHR) and improve data quality using natural language processing(NLP) and prostate-specific antigen-(PSA) based algorithms. Materials and MethodsWe built a data pipeline to transform UTMB Epic EHR data for patients identified through the Galveston Cancer Registry (2010-2021) into OMOP Common Data Model (CDM) v5.4. Data quality was assessed by comparing the OMOP-standardized data with Galveston Cancer Registry data using availability agreement, Cohens kappa and Intraclass Correlation Coefficient. NLP was used to extract PSA, Gleason score, and cancer stage from clinical text, and PSA-based algorithms were used to identify missing treatment and biochemical recurrence. ResultsWe extracted 815 analytic cases from UTMB EHR. Among them, 700 (85.9%) were complete and concordant with the cancer registry. PSA showed excellent value agreement. Structured Gleason score and stage data were sparse (n<20), but NLP greately improved capture. Treatment agreement was good compared with the cancer registry and improved slightly for radical prostatectomy after applying a PSA-based algorithm. Using PSA trajectories, we identified 60 cases of biochemical recurrence. DiscussionThe OMOP-standardized data from UTMB showed good agreement with the cancer registry. However, structured EHR fields incompletely captured diagnosis, pathology, and treatment details. NLP and PSA-based algorithms substantially improved data capture. Manual review also revealed errors in registry data, showing that OMOP-standardized EHR data can complement and help improve cancer registry quality. Conclusion: OMOP standardization combined with NLP and PSA-based algorithms improved prostate cancer data quality and research readiness. Lay SummaryElectronic health record (EHR) systems contain valuable long-term health information about cancer, but their use is limited by difficulties in data extraction, the lack of standard data formats, and missing information in structured fields. In this study, we built a data pipeline to convert EHR data into the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model, a widely used standard format that facilitates data sharing and collaborative research. To address missing data, we used natural language processing (NLP, a computational technique that enables computers to interpret human language) to extract prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, Gleason scores (a measure of cancer aggressiveness), and cancer stages from unstructured clinical notes. We also applied algorithms that track PSA blood trends over time to identify unrecorded cancer treatments and detect cancer recurrence. Comparing this database with a cancer registry demonstrated that standardized EHR records provide accurate clinical information and long-term follow-up. While structured EHR fields lacked key tumor characteristics, NLP dramatically improved their capture. Tracking PSA trends identified previously unrecorded treatments and flagged 60 potential cancer recurrences. Overall, combining standardized EHR formats with NLP and PSA-based algorithms creates a rich database to support real-world prostate cancer research.

infographic.key_insight: Standardizing prostate cancer EHR data to OMOP and adding NLP/PSA-based algorithms substantially improved capture of key clinical details and research readiness.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach can make real-world prostate cancer data more reliable for outcomes research, registry validation, and future precision oncology studies.
method: Transformed UTMB Epic EHR records for registry-identified prostate cancer patients into OMOP CDM v5.4.
Used NLP to extract PSA, Gleason score, and cancer stage from clinical notes.
Applied PSA-based algorithms to identify missing treatments and biochemical recurrence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of 815 analytic cases, 700 (85.9%) were complete and concordant with the cancer registry, with excellent PSA agreement and improved capture of sparse structured pathology/staging data after NLP.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on data quality, local documentation patterns, and manual validation; registry and EHR records can still contain errors or missing fields.
infographic.paper_title: Developing an OMOP-Standardized Prostate Cancer Database and Improving Data Quality Using NLP and PSA-Based Algorithms

title: Language eligibility criteria and enrolled racial and ethnic composition in US clinical trials: a cross-sectional study
authors: Tolas, A.; Du, L. Y.; Schutz, N.; Schmiedmayer, P.; O'Sullivan, J. W.; Johnson, A.; Longenecker, C. K.; Sarraju, A.; Rodriguez, F.; Yang, E.; Kim, D. S.
abstract: BACKGROUNDFederal policy now requires sponsors to submit diversity action plans for clinical trials, yet the modifiable features of trial design associated with enrolled composition remain poorly characterized. English-language proficiency requirements are written into eligibility criteria and recorded as free text in a public registry, making them visible and, in principle, amenable to revision, but their relationship to enrolled composition has been examined only within single disease areas and in small samples of trials. We examined whether these requirements and documented language accommodation were associated with the racial and ethnic composition of enrolled participants. METHODS AND FINDINGSWe conducted a cross-sectional study of interventional trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with at least one US site and posted results, using a registry snapshot retrieved in October 2026. The primary cohort comprised the 44,487 trials with exclusively US sites, of which 21,924 (49.3%) reported baseline race and 17,434 (39.2%) reported baseline ethnicity with counts that reconciled with the posted denominator. Both exposures were classified from free-text eligibility criteria using regular expressions validated against independent physician review of 150 trials. For the English-language requirement classifier, sensitivity was 88.2% and specificity was 99.2%. The outcome was the trial-level proportion of enrolled participants in each category, analyzed using generalized linear models adjusted for intervention class, therapeutic area, sponsor, phase, enrollment, sites, start year, US Census region, and the population composition of the trials site states. An English-language proficiency requirement appeared in 5,736 trials (12.9%); its prevalence rose from 7.4% of trials starting in 2010 to 26.2% in 2023 (odds ratio [OR] per decade 2.91, P<0.001), whereas documented accommodation, an eligibility statement allowing participation in a language other than English (Spanish in 99.9% of flagged trials), remained rare (788 trials, 1.8%). The requirement was associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.77-0.93, P=0.001) and Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.79-0.91, P<0.001), with no evidence of an association for White participants (OR=0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.04, P=0.75). Documented accommodation was associated with a higher proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=3.23, 95% CI 2.82-3.71, P<0.001). Geographic adjustment did not change the statistical significance of the requirement associations and attenuated the accommodation association. The main limitations were the cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inference; the restriction of enrollment analyses to trials reporting baseline demographics, which were more recent than those without such reporting; and possible misclassification of automatically classified exposures. CONCLUSIONSEnglish-language proficiency requirements became more than three times as common between 2010 and 2023 and were associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian and Hispanic/Latinx participants. Less common documented language accommodation was associated with a higher enrolled proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants. Because these criteria are investigator-written and publicly recorded, they may be a tractable target for improving enrollment equity, although whether revising them changes who enrolls requires prospective evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: Trials with English-language eligibility requirements enrolled fewer Asian and Hispanic/Latinx participants, while language accommodation was uncommon.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Adding explicit language accommodations to trial criteria could be a practical way to improve representation in US clinical trial enrollment.
method: Cross-sectional analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov interventional trials with at least one US site and posted results.
Eligibility criteria were mined with regular expressions to detect English-language requirements and language accommodations.
Associations with enrolled race/ethnicity proportions were modeled with adjustments for trial and site characteristics.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 44,487 US-only trials, an English-language requirement appeared in 12.9% and was associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian and Hispanic/Latinx participants; language accommodation was documented in only 1.8% of trials.
infographic.watch_item: This is an observational registry study, so the associations do not prove causation and may be influenced by incomplete race/ethnicity reporting in some trials.
infographic.paper_title: Language eligibility criteria and enrolled racial and ethnic composition in US clinical trials: a cross-sectional study

title: Personalised normative cardiac phenotyping reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity in cardiac shape and outcome risk
authors: Li, Z.; Bai, W.; Matthews, P. M.; Kainz, B.; Qiao, M.
abstract: Standard cardiac biomarkers such as ejection fraction, ventricular volumes, and strain compress complex three-dimensional heart dynamics into a small set of predefined measurements, leaving clinically important heterogeneity unrecognised. Here we propose a personalised normative cardiac frame-work in which each individual is compared to a digital twin representing expected healthy cardiac function given their age, sex, and body habitus. We show that structured patterns of deviation from these normative twins, discovered through systematic exploration of a generative cardiac dynamics space, constitute novel dynamic phenotypes that are not captured by conventional biomarkers. Applied independently to two UK Biobank cardiac cohorts with distinct shape representation, a 128-dimensional four-chamber statistical shape descriptor (HeartSSM, n = 52,365) and a 64-dimensional deep generative latent space from a conditional variational mesh autoencoder (MeshHeart cVAE, n = up to 39,376), we identify reproducible, continuous deviation-from-normative-twin scores (three discrete deviation phenotypes in the HeartSSM cohort) that improve cardiovascular risk stratification beyond ejection fraction, ventricular volumes, myocardial mass, and strain. The strongest effect was seen for incident atrial fibrillation among individuals with preserved ejection fraction ([≥]50%): incremental C-index {Delta}C = +0.068 (5-fold cross-validated {Delta}C = +0.063; likelihood-ratio P = 3.3 x 10-8), with a separate, smaller effect for incident stroke in the same preserved-EF subgroup in the independent MeshHeart cVAE representation (which showed no signal for atrial fibrillation) ({Delta}C = +0.024, P = 2.6 x 10-4). Both effects were checked against placebo controls in which the deviation scores were replaced by Gaussian noise. To test whether the normative twin generalises beyond UK Biobanks specific scanning and processing pipeline, we applied the MeshHeart cVAE normative twin, unmodified, to an independent external cohort of healthy volunteers imaged at a different hospital (Gen-Scan/Hammersmith, n = 315): deviation scores in this cohort were of comparable magnitude to the UK Biobank healthy reference (ratio of means = 1.09; Mann-Whitney P = 1.4 x 10-5), indicating that the normative twin captures cross-site-transferable structure rather than a scanner- or pipeline-specific artefact. Our findings suggest that cardiac phenotyping can move beyond predefined measurements toward data-driven dynamic phenotypes that better capture the heterogeneity underlying cardiovascular disease risk, even among individuals whose ejection fraction appears normal.

infographic.key_insight: Personalised “normative twin” cardiac models reveal hidden, reproducible patterns of heart-shape deviation that identify clinically relevant risk beyond standard measurements like ejection fraction and strain.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could improve risk stratification—especially for atrial fibrillation in people with preserved ejection fraction—by spotting abnormal cardiac phenotypes that conventional biomarkers miss.
method: Built age-, sex-, and body-habitus-matched digital twins of expected healthy cardiac function.
Compared individuals against two independent shape representations: HeartSSM (128D) and MeshHeart cVAE (64D).
Derived deviation-from-norm scores and tested whether they improved prediction of outcomes beyond standard cardiac biomarkers.
infographic.evidence_signal: In UK Biobank cohorts, deviation scores improved cardiovascular risk prediction, with the strongest signal for incident atrial fibrillation in preserved-EF participants (ΔC up to +0.068; LR P = 3.3 × 10^-8), plus a smaller independent stroke signal in the MeshHeart cVAE cohort; placebo noise controls were negative.
infographic.watch_item: Generalizability and deployment need careful validation across imaging protocols and external populations, since signals varied by representation and some outcomes appeared only in one cohort/model.
infographic.paper_title: Personalised normative cardiac phenotyping reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity in cardiac shape and outcome risk

title: Decision models can offload structured clinical tasks from large language models
authors: Ariel, D.; Laban, G.; Endelman, S.; Balicer, R.; Dagan, N.; Cohen, S.
abstract: Decision models like Jev read text and return probabilities, categories, or ordinal levels, with confidence scores for the latter two, at a fraction of large language models (LLMs) cost. We explored how Jev could be integrated into clinical workflows for all these output types: mortality risk estimation, categorical Choosing-Wisely decisions for patient questions, and ordinal colon cancer staging. With standard LLM-style inputs, Jev trailed five flagship LLMs: mortality AUROC was 0.822 versus 0.837-0.846; Choosing-Wisely accuracy, 87.7% versus 98.4-100%; and staging accuracy, 45.4% versus 94.2-100%. Developer-recommended input alterations improved staging accuracy to 75.8% with medical context, 82.1% with task decomposition, and 85.8% with both. None of Jevs staging errors had full confidence. Using Jev for fully confident staging decisions and LLMs for the rest was non-inferior to each LLM alone and cut flagship LLM costs by 33-44%. Prompted as designed, decision models may efficiently share structured clinical tasks with LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Decision models can handle structured clinical subtasks cheaply, while LLMs remain stronger for harder or less certain cases.
infographic.clinical_relevance: A hybrid workflow that routes confident structured decisions to a decision model and the rest to an LLM could reduce cost without sacrificing performance.
method: Compared a decision model (Jev) with five flagship LLMs on three clinical tasks.
Tasks included mortality risk prediction, Choosing-Wisely category decisions, and ordinal colon cancer staging.
Tested standard prompting plus developer-guided input changes such as added context and task decomposition.
infographic.evidence_signal: On standard inputs, Jev underperformed LLMs, but with improved prompting it reached 75.8% to 85.8% staging accuracy; routing only fully confident staging cases to Jev made the hybrid approach non-inferior and cut LLM costs by 33% to 44%.
infographic.watch_item: The hybrid approach depends on reliable confidence calibration and may not transfer equally well across tasks or settings without careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Decision models can offload structured clinical tasks from large language models

title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
authors: Rohani, F.; Mostafavi, S.; Ebrahimifakhar, P.; Zomorrodi, R.; Mueller, A.
abstract: BackgroundAttention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. MethodsThis study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. ResultsAmong the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. ConclusionsThe proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

infographic.key_insight: A multi-domain EEG model that combines spectral, connectivity, and topological features can classify ADHD at the subject level more accurately than single-feature approaches.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This work supports the development of non-invasive, explainable EEG-based tools that may aid future ADHD screening and biomarker research.
method: Preprocessed EEG from 121 subjects and split it into overlapping windows for feature extraction.
Built 1,043 features across spectral, wPLI functional connectivity, and persistent homology domains, then reduced them to 110 using RFE.
Compared SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and MLP with stratified 5-fold cross-validation and used SHAP/LIME for interpretability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The best model was SVM, with 80.17% accuracy, 80.95% F1-score, 80.14% balanced accuracy, 86.72% ROC-AUC, and 87.34% PR-AUC.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was based on a relatively small single-study cohort, so external validation and real-world robustness testing are still needed.
infographic.paper_title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification

title: AI-Assisted Tissue-Based Antibody Interpretation in Autoimmune Encephalitis: Prospective Validation and Reader Study
authors: Cao, Z.; Xie, D.; Zou, S.; Li, D.; Martinez-Martinez, P.; Zong, S.; Zhang, Z.
abstract: Tissue-based assays provide broad screening for neural autoantibodies but remain vulnerable to technical and reader-dependent variability. We evaluated an integrated workflow combining automated 3,3'-diaminobenzidine tissue-based assay processing, digital whole-slide imaging, and interpretable deep learning. Model development used 2,357 retrospective serum and cerebrospinal fluid images referred from more than 80 institutions and processed in a centralized laboratory, with reference labels established by expert-consensus tissue-based assay interpretation. A prospective validation cohort included 200 images from 200 unique patients (154 positive and 46 negative; 100 serum and 100 cerebrospinal fluid). The same images were evaluated by two expert and two novice readers in a fixed-order two-round study, with unaided interpretation followed by artificial-intelligence-assisted interpretation after a washout of at least two weeks. The standalone binary classifier achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.922, accuracy of 86.5%, sensitivity of 85.7%, and specificity of 89.1% in prospective validation. Pooled reader accuracy was 90.4% in the unaided round and 97.4% in the artificial-intelligence-assisted round (McNemar P < 0.001), with specificity of 82.6% and 99.5%, respectively. Novice-reader accuracy was 83.3% unaided and 96.5% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001), approaching unaided expert accuracy of 97.5%. Among tissue-based-assay-positive cases, reader accuracy for cytoplasmic/nuclear antigen-associated versus neural surface antigen-associated staining-pattern subclassification was 88.8% unaided and 94.0% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001). These findings support further multicentre, cross-platform evaluation of artificial-intelligence-assisted neural autoantibody tissue interpretation. Abbreviated summaryCao et al. report prospective validation of an automated tissue-based neural autoantibody workflow combining digital imaging and interpretable deep learning. Artificial-intelligence-assisted reading was associated with higher interpretation accuracy, particularly among less-experienced readers, supporting further multicentre validation across laboratories and imaging platforms.

infographic.key_insight: An AI-assisted digital workflow for tissue-based autoantibody interpretation improved accuracy and consistency in autoimmune encephalitis screening, especially for less-experienced readers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help laboratories reduce reader-dependent variability and improve confidence in neural autoantibody testing, supporting more reliable diagnostic workflows.
method: Trained on 2,357 retrospective serum and CSF tissue-based assay images from >80 institutions
Validated prospectively on 200 unique-patient images with expert consensus reference labels
Compared unaided vs AI-assisted interpretation by two experts and two novices in a two-round reader study
infographic.evidence_signal: In prospective validation, the standalone classifier reached AUROC 0.922 with 86.5% accuracy, and AI assistance raised pooled reader accuracy from 90.4% to 97.4% (McNemar P < 0.001).
infographic.watch_item: Results came from centralized, expert-reviewed images in a single workflow, so broader multicenter and cross-platform validation is still needed before routine deployment.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Assisted Tissue-Based Antibody Interpretation in Autoimmune Encephalitis: Prospective Validation and Reader Study
